flashcards.q: What are the three mechanisms for getting structured output from an LLM, and how do they relate?
flashcards.a: Prompt-and-validate (ask for JSON, parse with pydantic, no guarantee), constrained decoding (schema compiled to grammar, per-step logit masking, invalid output impossible), and repair loops (validation error fed back, bounded retries, salvage). They are stacked, not alternatives: constrain machine-facing fields, validate even under constraint.

flashcards.q: OpenAI Structured Outputs: when launched, and what are the headline adherence numbers?
flashcards.a: Launched 2024-08-06. gpt-4o-2024-08-06 with Structured Outputs: 100% schema adherence on their evals; 93% trained-only without the mask; gpt-4-0613 prompting alone: under 40%.

flashcards.q: How does constrained decoding work mechanically, below 'it masks logits'?
flashcards.a: Compile once: JSON Schema -> CFG -> pushdown automaton; compute per-state which of the ~128K vocab tokens keep the prefix valid (>99% context-independent, precomputed into a token-mask cache; remainder checked at runtime against a persistent stack). Decode: after each token, advance the automaton, apply -inf mask to invalid logits, softmax, sample — invalid tokens get probability exactly 0.

flashcards.q: What can a JSON Schema grammar enforce, and what can it never enforce?
flashcards.a: Can: types, required keys, key sets (additionalProperties:false), scalar enums, formats/simple regex, nesting via $ref/anyOf. Never: semantic correctness of values (wrong-but-valid enum pick), cross-field constraints (grammars are positional, not relational), or constraints outside the provider subset — those either 400 or get silently stripped by SDK transforms into descriptions.

flashcards.q: Why did OpenAI compile schemas to a CFG instead of an FSM, and what does it cost?
flashcards.a: FSMs cannot count brackets — recursive schemas (e.g. children: {$ref: '#'}) need a pushdown stack. Cost: PDA states are not fully precomputable (infinitely many stack configurations), which is why mask computation needed the context-independent/context-dependent split, and CFG masking measured ~10x slower than JSON-schema masking in XGrammar benchmarks (JSON schemas are mostly regular).

flashcards.q: Name the four holes in the 100% schema-adherence claim.
flashcards.a: (1) Refusal — safety path bypasses the grammar, you get a 200, billed, schema broken (OpenAI refusal field / Anthropic stop_reason refusal). (2) Truncation — max_tokens cut mid-array, finish_reason length, unparseable. (3) The subset — guarantee covers a documented subset; unsupported keywords 400 or silently strip. (4) Scope — adherence says nothing about value correctness; schema-conformant wrong answers are within spec.

flashcards.q: What is the format tax, and where does most of it live?
flashcards.a: Format restrictions measurably degrade reasoning (stricter = worse; JSON worst — closed brackets force structural commitment before content decisions). The Format Tax (2026) localized most of the loss to the format-requesting instructions in the PROMPT, not the decoder mask (decoder adds ~-0.03 bits further diversity compression). Closed-weight recent models measured near tax-free; open-weight models still pay — measure per model.

flashcards.q: Constrained decoding overhead: quote two contrasting measured numbers and reconcile them.
flashcards.a: Near-zero: XGrammar precomputes >99% of the mask (3.5x/10x faster masking, up to 14x/80x end-to-end on flat JSON). Far-from-zero: 3.6x-8.2x latency overhead measured on 7-9B models in some settings; cardinality wall — vLLM at batch 256 over 10K-value choice sets measured 7.5 req/s vs 219 req/s with precomputed trie masks (29x). Reconciliation: overhead is a function of schema class, batch size (CPU masking bottlenecks exactly when GPU throughput peaks), and cache temperature, plus 10-60s first-request compile.

flashcards.q: What are the four design decisions of a repair loop, with the numbers?
flashcards.a: (1) Bounded retries — cap 3 (instructor default max_retries=3); each retry is a full inference pass, unbounded loops are the classic cost incident. (2) Error messages that teach — loc + msg naming the field and the fix. (3) Change something between retries — identical re-ask can reproduce the same failure (same-error thrash). (4) A salvage path — field-level regex extraction, nulls for the rest, needs_review flag, human queue.

flashcards.q: Anthropic structured outputs: what is in the supported subset, and what 400s?
flashcards.a: In: basic types, scalar enums, const, anyOf/allOf (limits), $ref/$defs, required + additionalProperties:false, ten string formats (date-time, time, date, duration, email, hostname, uri, ipv4, ipv6, uuid), minItems 0 or 1 only. 400s: recursive schemas, minimum/maximum/multipleOf, minLength/maxLength, external $ref, enum of complex types, regex backreferences/lookarounds/\b. Property ordering: required first, then optional.

flashcards.q: What is the Constrained Decoding Attack (CDA) result, and what does it mean for user-supplied schemas?
flashcards.a: CCS 2026: grammar-enforced fields are a control-plane injection channel. DictAttack decouples jailbreak payload across prompt and dictionary grammar — 94.3-99.5% attack success rate on flagship models (gpt-5, gemini-2.5-pro, deepseek-r1), still 75.8% against SOTA jailbreak guardrails. User-supplied schemas must be audited like SQL: allowlist keywords, cap enum cardinality and pattern complexity.

flashcards.q: When should you NOT use constrained decoding?
flashcards.a: Tiny fixed vocabularies (3-value sentiment: membership check beats a CFG). One-shot human-facing prose (the tax is paid, nothing gained — even *requesting* JSON narrows which answer you get). Cold schemas on tight latency SLOs (10-60s first compile). Cross-field/value semantics (grammar is positional, not relational — use code validation + repair loop). Open-weight models on reasoning-heavy tasks before measuring the tax.
